VERDICT: ACCEPT

I checked the answer against small cases rather than a full proof of the lower bound.

**Case r = 2 (verified).** Trees of maximum degree 2 are paths. Taking the first cut in path 1 at its midpoint, with sides L and R, and choosing the second cut in path 2 as a prefix of size n/2 with a elements in L, gives max(a, n/2 − a) ≥ n/4 for any pair of paths. A uniformly random pair of orders gives M ≈ n/4, since the cell products satisfy P·S ≤ 1/16 and Q·R ≤ 1/16. So f(2,2) = 1/4, which matches 1/(r+2) and rules out 1/(r+1).

**Case r = 3 (partial check).** The proposed spider construction with legs (2c, 2c, c) on both trees, with c = 1/5, has every leg-intersection of size at most c, and every leg-difference Q also at most c. Since every cut set is a tip of a single leg, this gives M ≤ 1/5, so f(3,2) ≤ 1/5. I also tested a natural competitor, legs (1/2, 1/4, 1/4) against (1/3, 1/3, 1/3), which satisfies the full-leg constraints at c = 1/6. Partial tips of the long leg push M to at least 2/9, so that configuration does not beat 1/5.

**Gaps.** The lower bound M ≥ n/(r+2) for general r is asserted via an unspecified "centroid branch" argument, which I could not verify. Non-spider trees and other constructions were not ruled out. The formula also matches the r = 1 analogue f(r,1) = 1/r, which is a mild sign of a consistent pattern.

The evidence supports 1/(r+2), but the lower bound is unproven, so my confidence is moderate.

CONFIDENCE: 3
